work.author: Augustine
work.title: Libellus Adversus Fulgentium Donatistam
work.edition: Machine translation (claude-opus-5-5, Patristica, 2026-11-27) of: CSEL 53, ed. Michael Petschenig (1910); OGL csel-dev opp-lat1; scan: https://archive.org/stream/CSEL53#page/n429/mode/2up

paragraphs.text: I did not scorn the little book which your reverence, brother Fulgentius, sent me, and I accepted it. Whether you composed it yourself or got it from somewhere else no longer much concerns me. For this too is a duty of our religion: not to look at persons, but to seek the truth in all things, to recognize it when found, and to guard it once recognized. So the apostle Paul says: "Test all things; hold fast what is good; abstain from every form of evil." I will therefore state briefly what you spread out at length and with some ingenuity in your writing. You said that there is one baptism, which the Samaritan, that is, the heretic, did not deserve to have; that the one enclosed garden, which is the Church, has a sealed fountain which no outsider touches; and that there is one oil, the most holy chrism, which dying flies corrupt and which sinners will in no way give. Against these points I must prepare my reply with the Lord's help, and take it from nowhere else than the divine reading. Let us now take the beginning of the word; or rather, let us hold fast to the Word himself, the beginning of the laws, the Lord, the leader and prince of the heavenly army. Let us wage war, and with the trumpet consecrated by his hand let us attack the mighty walls of the wicked city of Jericho. That is, let us surround the height of worldly wisdom with the Lord's testaments, let us sound out with the voices of truth and freedom, let us compel our adversaries to take refuge in the house of Rahab, that is, of the Church, which receives his messengers, because of the destruction of the world, and let us condemn the obstinate with anathema, so that we may be victors to the end. These things, then, you have taken from the law against the law, from God's testament against God's testament, from the fountain of truth against the fountain of truth, as though [?] they were a strong barrier at first sight, as if truth could be overcome by itself, or the glory of light darkened by its own brightness.

The Donatist said: Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, the teacher and guardian of the one baptism, so that the mind's error might not lead thirsty souls to dry cisterns, proclaimed that the never-failing draughts are his own and testified in his Gospel, saying: "Whoever thirsts, let him come and drink; whoever believes in me, as Isaiah says."

The Catholic replied: It does not say "as Isaiah says," but "as the scripture says." But I will pass over such things as mere obstacles, so as not to shut out the reader's profit with a long discourse.

The Donatist said: "Whoever believes in me, as Isaiah said, rivers of living water will flow from his belly." And so that it might not be said that one can drink anywhere and everywhere, he himself distinguished the merits of the waters when he condemned the origin of Samaria's apostasy at its own well: "Whoever drinks of this water," he says, "will thirst again; whoever drinks of the water that I shall give will never thirst, but it will become in him a fountain of water springing up to eternal life."

The Catholic replied: You put this forward, of course, in order to show that we Catholics are like Samaritans and without baptism. So now begin to see the Donatists in the Samaritans. The teaching of the Samaritans, as the book of Kings tells us, was this: they feared God and at the same time worshiped idols; they kept the divine law and did not in the least abandon the errors of their fathers; they had the sign of circumcision and did not keep fellowship with the Israelites. You do the same. You fear God and at the same time worship an idol of clay, Donatus (for he too was fashioned from earth); you keep the divine law and do not abandon the error of your fathers; you have the sacrament of baptism and do not wish to have fellowship with the Catholics. See, you resemble them in every respect. Just as the circumcision of the Samaritans could not then be given a second time, so now the baptism of the Donatists must not be repeated, as the Lord Christ teaches: "He who has once been washed has no need to be washed again." For the circumcision of the Samaritans signifies the baptism of the Donatists, as the apostle says: "You were circumcised with a circumcision not made with hands, in stripping off the body of the flesh, but in the circumcision of Christ, buried with him in baptism." As for the Lord's words, "Whoever drinks of this water will thirst again," he was speaking not of baptism but of the earthly element. For if he had meant to point to baptism here, he would never have asked the Samaritan woman for a drink. Besides, that well was not called Samaria's, but Jacob's; and Jacob was certainly no heretic, but beloved of God, always dear to him; and he himself drank from it, and his sons, and his cattle.

The Donatist said: Never, then, does the Spirit of the Church allow to be joined to it what has deserved to be denounced by the divine mouth, as the proclamation of the law warns beforehand: "Two and two, one against one"; and the Lord in the Gospel: "Then two will be in the field; one will be taken and one left. Two women grinding at the mill; one will be taken and one left." You see, then, that there are two kinds of baptism and two rewards of merit: the one is scorched by the heat of a deadly disposition, and a soaking thirst dries up its never-failing draughts; the other, once it has been drunk down the channels, satisfies thirst with the everlastingness of life. Surely he shows perpetual drought in dug-out pools, and in shutting off from them the merit of life he has opened the way to death, as Jeremiah says: "This people has done two evils. They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water"; and again: "Let all who forsake you be put to shame; let those who depart from you be written in the book of death; because they have forsaken you, let those who depart from you, the fountain of life, be put to shame."

The Catholic replied: You set one against one; I assert many baptisms against the one. For the pagan baptizes, and the Jew baptizes, and the Sadducee baptizes, and many outside the rule of the law that was given do not cease to baptize. But the one baptism is the one that is true; the true one is Christ's; Christ's is that of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. This is the true one, this is the saving one; nothing can be compared to it. Whoever does not receive it has himself shut off from himself the merit of life and opened the way to death.

The Donatist said: But if, as you claim, one faith stands in both, why did he distinguish between faithful water and faithless water with a just separation, as the Lord testifies through Isaiah: "Who has told you that the fire burns? Who has told you of that everlasting place? He who walks in righteousness, who proclaims the right way, who hates crime and injustice, who keeps his hands from bribes, who stops his ear so as not to hear the judgment of blood, and shuts his eyes so that they do not see iniquity: he will dwell in lofty hope; strong bread will be given him, and his water will be faithful." And separating faithless water from its faithfulness, he put it thus, as Jeremiah testifies: "Why do those who wrong me prevail? My wound has become hard: how shall I heal it? It has become to me like lying water that has no faithfulness."

The Catholic replied: Although all heretics disagree among themselves in their teaching, in the handing down of baptism they agree in the solemn formula, just as among the Jews and the Samaritans of old there was one circumcision but different faiths. So it must be done now for converts as it was then: what is bound by teaching alone should be loosed again by teaching alone, so that they may hear from the Lord: "You are already clean because of the word that I have spoken to you; abide in me, and I in you." For all these things happened to them as a figure, but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.

The Donatist said: Ezekiel too speaks thus: "And they saw that there are many who turned away the water of the ancient pool, and they did not look to him who made it from the beginning, and they did not see him who founded it." Unheard-of madness of the faithless, neither willing to believe the divine voices nor willing to keep the apostle's simple teaching in the jaws of their error!

The Catholic replied: Far be it, far be it from us to draw off the water of the ancient pool into a faction, as you do, or not to believe the divine oracles. What we read we believe, and what we believe we preach. Hear what our origin is and where its water has been poured out. In Zechariah you have this: "Living waters will go out from Jerusalem, half of them to the eastern sea and half of them to the farthest sea" (that is, from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth); "in summer and in winter they will be" (that is, they will be at all times); "and the Lord will be king over all the earth"; that is, Christ will rule over all the earth, not Donatus. This is the possession, this the inheritance of Christ, which is tended by the saints and watered by the never-failing fountain, of which it was said to him: "I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession." Whoever is in it has been enrolled as an heir; whoever is not in it is already condemned and destined for death, as the scripture says: "Whoever goes out of the doors of your house will be guilty on his own head."

The Donatist said: Hence God proclaims that he has one baptism; hence the apostle confirms that he has told everyone there is one, as God proves through Solomon: "An enclosed garden, my sister, my bride, a sealed fountain, a well of living water, a paradise with the fruit of apples."

The Catholic replied: Remember the law and pay careful attention, and see that from this paradise, from this enclosed garden, from this sealed fountain, the wave of salvation runs down outside as well, and it goes against the Assyrians, that is, against you Donatists. For it is from the Assyrians that those Samaritans are born to whom you have been compared. "This," says the scripture, "is the river that goes against the Assyrians," against the nation hostile to God's people. It does not go for them, but against them. For to some it is the odor of death unto death, but to others the odor of life unto life. For just as he who eats and drinks the Lord's blood unworthily eats and drinks judgment on himself, so he who receives baptism unworthily receives judgment on himself, not salvation. For Judas the traitor received the good body, and Simon Magus the good baptism of Christ; but because they did not use the good well, by using it badly they were destroyed as wicked men. Baptism is good, Christ's blood and body are good, the law too is good, but only if one uses them lawfully. Nor is it not divine because it is also outside, nor will it be thought foreign because it is held by outsiders, nor will it be condemned by us justly because it is handled unjustly by the wicked. The water of paradise is the water of the Trinity. Where we recognize it, we do not deny that it is paradise's; where we do not discern it, we do not say at all that it is paradise's. Whatever has arisen outside must in no way be called paradise's: for example, the Manichee, since he was never in paradise and did not go out of the Church as you did, is not to be thought to have the water of paradise, because he arose outside. Such a one needs to live, lest he die for ever; but in order to live lawfully, let him live in the Church itself [?], lest he eat and drink judgment.

The Donatist said: On the contrary, the apostle testifies that he said: "One God, one faith, one baptism." There is no variation in divine teaching; in all things the servant follows the Lord; in nothing does the disciple differ from the master.

The Catholic replied: Whom are you following, whom are you imitating, whom do you consider the author of this outrage? Give me any one of the saints who rebaptized after the Trinity, as you do. Read me not those writings by whose authority I am not bound, but the writings of the New and Old Testaments, to which we are both subject. If there is one baptism, why do you double the one? For what you repeat is nothing other than what you find to be true. Since, then, as he said, you are rebuilding what you destroyed, you show yourselves to be transgressors.

The Donatist said: Or if you think the sacrament of baptism is one even when joined by some mixing with the guilty, hear from the prophets by whom it is rightly dispensed, as Solomon says: "The fountain of life is in the hands of the just."

The Catholic replied: The Lord, who foresaw your error, spoke well of you: "You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts; for what is exalted among men is an abomination before God." If you are just and the fountain of life is in your hand, you are not a man but God. Let people take refuge in you, let them believe in you, let all hope of life be placed in you, let baptism itself be given in your name, and let nothing be said of the Lord! Do you want to know where to look for this fountain of life? You have it in the psalm: "With you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light." Have you not read: "An evil son has proud eyes; an evil son calls himself just, but does not wash away his own going out"? Unless you recognize that, as a man, you are guilty, unless you cry out with a truthful heart that you are a sinner, you can in no way be justified, as the prophet says: "Declare your iniquities, that you may be justified." And the apostle John: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us."
The Donatist said: And David says: "But let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head with fatness."

The Catholic replied: Then give me any one of your people whom you can prove not to be a sinner, so that your oil cannot be a sinner's oil, since it is written: "There is no man who does not sin." You interpret badly; read what comes just above, so that you can grasp the sense. It says: "The just man will correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head." That is: merciful rebuke is better than smooth flattery, as in that other saying: "Better are the wounds of a friend than the willing kisses of an enemy." The oil of the sinner is the flatterer's coaxing, of which it says elsewhere: "His words are softer than oil, yet they are darts." The oil of the just is the Spirit of God, as Peter says: "Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit." So stop calling the Holy Spirit the oil of a sinner, lest you begin to declare that God is a sinner.

The Donatist said: In this passage the confection of the faithless is plainly shown, which is polluted when it is touched with hostile presumption by a criminal priest, and whose sacrifice, like the oil, is rejected by the divine voice. "The criminal," it says, "who sacrifices a calf to me is like one who kills a dog; he who offers fine flour is like one who offers pig's blood; and he who offers incense as a memorial is like a blasphemer."

The Catholic replied: It is certain that God curses and despises the burnt offerings of priest and people alike if a good conscience is not present. Or if you want this to be understood as said of priests alone, how is it that among you the confection of criminal priests is not polluted? You say: "As long as the wicked are hidden they cannot defile, because it is written: 'What is hidden is mine; what is manifest is yours.'" If, then, the wicked cannot defile as long as they are hidden, why are you not afraid to rebaptize distant nations to whom the names of Donatus and Caecilian are unknown? Which of you ever brought anyone's evil deeds to their knowledge? And even if he had brought them and had not proved them, it would do them no harm at all, according to the saying: "What is hidden is mine; what is manifest is yours."

The Donatist said: The prophet Habakkuk further makes his waters known by the Spirit: "You set your horses in the sea," he says, "troubling many waters. The city of Gilead despised me, which works folly, troubling the waters. And your strength is like that of a pirate."

The Catholic replied: Recognize your own weapons turned against you, as it is written: "Let their sword enter their own hearts, and let their bow be broken." Your strength, Donatist, is like that of a pirate: by force you rebaptize, by force you fight in the water, by force you kill in the water. Doing such things you will be captured and slain as a pirate, unless you are converted, repent, and serve as a soldier of Christ the King in the Catholic Church.

The Donatist said: If, then, the Church glories in a single fountain, surely it is the cave of the traitors that exalts itself in a multitude of waters and, confused with the drunkenness of its baptism, commits fornication with kings, as John says: "Come, I will show you the condemnation of the great harlot who sits upon many waters, and all who dwell on the earth have become drunk with the wine of her fornication." I ask, what are the many waters but many baptisms? What is the harlot but the cave of the traitors, which serves, in bondage, the pleasures of kings, from whom she drinks the cup of persecution, and in her drunken blindness mixes it for the peoples and leads into madness those whom she has watered? The most wise Solomon forbade approaching her: "Keep away from strange water," he says, "and do not drink from a strange fountain, so that you may live a long time, and years of life will be added to you. Let the fountain of your water be your own: let no stranger share it with you." So the only one who does not have a fountain of his own is the one who by the harlot's power possesses a multitude of waters. The apostle John too condemns the multitude of waters, saying: "And the angel said to me: The waters which you saw, on which that harlot sits, are peoples, crowds and nations."

The Catholic replied: As I see it, wherever water is named, whether in a bad or a good sense, you have taken it to be baptism. If in a good sense, you wanted to assign it to yourself; if in a bad sense, to me; so that what the apostle Paul said might be fulfilled in you: "understanding neither what they say nor the things about which they make assertions." For as Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so these resist the truth. The angel says: "The waters which you saw are peoples, crowds and nations." And you resist the angel's explanation and say: "I ask, what are the many waters but many baptisms? What is the harlot but the cave of the traitors?" If you want to learn the names of traitors too, you have your own: Silvanus of Cirta, handing over the sacred books to Felix the curator; Marinus of Aquae Tibilitanae, offering three codices to Romanus the curator; Victor of Rusicade, burning the four Gospels as though they were trifles [?]. These are the men who dared to condemn Caecilian, innocent and absent. This is the den of thieves, this the offspring of traitors, this the harlot who abandoned Christ and opened her brothels to Donatus; whose house, according to Solomon, is the retreat of death, whose ways are the ways of the underworld; who calls herself clean though she is full of filth, who proclaims herself innocent though she is entangled in crimes, who commits shameful acts and charges her own deeds to another, so as not to be the first to hear of what she has done. For you defame the Catholics with your own deeds, so as to separate the peoples from the Lord. And so, when you urge your people, as if they were yours, to keep away from our water, and say: "Keep away from strange water and do not drink from a strange fountain. Let the fountain of your water be your own: let no stranger share it with you," who does not see that the prophet was commending chastity to husbands and wives, and that you have strayed far from the truth? Or if no stranger ought to share your fountain, why do you go looking for strangers? Why do you rebaptize Catholics?

The Donatist said: It is clear, then, that the multitude of waters is among the traitors, where there are the various seeds of schisms, where the manifold plagues of the heretics, where the detestable dregs of the Manichees' filth, or [?] Charybdis saw those swept off into eternal death into the steep pool of a muddy whirlpool, and kindled the oil of destruction with devouring flames [?]. The Catholic replied: O what proof, O what error, O what raving [?]! "It is clear, then, that the multitude of waters is among the traitors, where there are the various seeds of schisms, where the manifold plagues of the heretics, where the detestable dregs of the Manichees' filth"? How do you prove that the manifold plagues of schismatics are with us? If they were with us, they would not be heretics but Catholics.

The Donatist said: Hear what Solomon says: "Dying flies destroy the sweet confection." The sweetness of oil, then, is natural to it, but if it is violated by a wicked touch it is polluted and becomes an unpleasant confection. And rightly has the Holy Spirit likened the traitors to unclean flying creatures, because they wickedly swoop down on another's table and foul the sweetness of the oil with their unclean touch.

The Catholic replied: Who violates it with a wicked touch? The one who preserves what he finds, or the one who shamelessly destroys what has been prepared? When did we touch your oil? When did we drive out the Holy Spirit by insulting [?] him? Show that any one of us has wickedly fallen into the oil of the divinity, or has unlawfully violated the baptism of the Trinity, as you do. The dying flies, the Donatists, buzz around all the members of the body; wherever they find a wound, they sting the healthy parts, lick the sick ones, and pour into their ulcers the worms of sins, which gnaw the conscience, which make an end of the soul, which feed corruption, and which do not spare even dead corpses. The dying flies, when they destroy the oil, are killed by the oil; for you who blow out the Holy Spirit are not alive.

The Donatist said: This is what the most holy David properly teaches, supplying the rule of our faith: that the sinner's oil brings no salvation and must not touch anyone's head. "Let not the oil of the sinner," he says, "anoint my head." So the person of the sinner must be sought out by careful examination, unless, as the profane assert, the Lord was not speaking of a sacrilegious priest.

The Catholic replied: You know you are guilty of sin, and yet you dare to say, "We must look to the person of the sinner"? Hear, then, who this person of the sinner is. The apostle said: "All have sinned and lack the glory of God." And Solomon: "There is no one among men who does not sin." And Job: "If he found wickedness in his angels, how much more in the sons of men, who have an earthly dwelling!" This is the person of the sinner: every human being is a sinner. If you are a priest, you are a man; and if you are a man, you are a sinner. Who do you make yourself out to be? You have said that you alone are holy, you alone are righteous, you alone are without sin, you alone are without stain. You have said that baptism is yours, the holy oil is yours, the Lord's table is yours, and all the things God grants to the faithful are yours. What is left, except that you wickedly and impiously declare yourself to be God? But hear what the very head of pride deserved to hear: "How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, you who rose in the morning, you who wounded the nations, you who said in your heart: I will ascend above heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God. I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north, and I will be like the Most High. But you shall go down to hell, to the depths of the pit." So unless you repent, unless you are converted, unless you lay aside your pride and ask pardon for your sins, you will hear what he heard, because, though you are a man, you make yourself God.

The Donatist said: In the same way, through the prophet Haggai, the Lord showed in a wholesome lesson that the touch of the unclean brings defilement, and that no polluted person can make anything holy if with unlawful presumption he tries to touch what he sees is held to be holy. He set the prophet before us as a warning: "Ask the priests," says the Lord, "and say: If a man binds holy flesh in the hem of his garment, and the hem of the garment touches any food, whether bread or wine or oil, is it made holy? And the priests answered and said: No. And the Lord said: If someone unclean in soul touches any of these, will it be defiled? And the priests said: It will be defiled. And the Lord said: So it is with this people, and so with this nation: everyone who approaches there will be defiled."

The Catholic replied: You have used this testimony against yourself, for you place the gift of God in your own power. For if the touch of the holy does not remove the defilement of the unclean, then all that you perform, all that you consecrate, all that you wash is in vain. "If," it says, "what is holy touches food, whether bread or wine or oil, will it be made holy? And the priests answered and said: No." Where then is that which you boast of, your claim that your holiness confers purity? Or if you are moved by the words, "So it is with this people, and so with this nation: everyone who approaches there will be defiled," then show us that Haggai, who taught these things, left the midst of that same people so that he too would not be polluted by being among them. That touching signifies works. If, it says, a holy man touches the unclean, the unclean will not be made holy; if an unclean man touches the holy, the holy will be defiled. That is: a holy man who is joined to this most wicked nation is more easily made wicked than the nation is changed for the better, because people run more readily to imitate the wicked than the mind is roused to the virtues of the good. In the same way, a little wormwood thrown into a great quantity of honey quickly turns it bitter, but even if twice as much honey is thrown into wormwood, its sweetness cannot prevail. We must go out from the midst of the wicked in mind, not in flesh; in works, not in bodies. "Do not take part," says the apostle, "in the unfruitful works of darkness." He says "works," not "altars." For it is written in Isaiah: "Those who say, Depart from me, do not come near me, for you are unclean — these shall be smoke in my wrath, a fire burning all day long." If the words of men do not frighten you, let at least the wrath of a threatening God turn you back.

The Donatist said: A robber never brought his plunder out into the light; those who work by night have always shrunk all the more fiercely from the light that all good people welcome. Only the traditor is not broken even by God's threats, and shamelessly glories in another's garment. Against him the Lord cries out through Zephaniah, and is not heard: "It shall be," he says, "on the day of the Lord's sacrifice, that I will punish the princes and all who are clothed in foreign garments."

The Catholic replied: I do not fear your charges, for my conscience is secure. Whoever you say handed over the Scriptures, show me the name and the place of that traditor. You will never be able to show it, just as you were never able to before. But even if you do produce someone, he cannot harm me, for the Lord says: "The soul of the father is mine, the soul of the son is mine. The soul that sins, it alone shall die." Yet I do not rejoice in another's garment, for I always exult in the Catholic faith. That is the garment I have, the one with which my merciful and kind Father clothed me in beauty on the day of my redemption: "Bring out," he says, "the best robe and put it on him, for this son of mine was dead and has come back to life; he was lost and is found." It is surely the same garment of which the apostle Paul said: "As many of you as have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ." This is the garment I have, in this I rejoice, in this I shall always appear more glorious. This is the garment that you have either stolen like robbers or, wretches that you are, soiled.

The Donatist said: For inasmuch as wickedness longs to build its wandering errors on the goods of others, and tries to cover the fogs of falsehood with a false "catholic," it walks along winding hills. The Lord stood against it and confronted it through Jeremiah: "Do not trust," he says, "in lying words, for they will profit you nothing at all, when you say: The temple of the Lord is the temple of God." And the Lord in Deuteronomy: "Take heed to yourself that you do not offer burnt offerings in every place you see, but in the place which the Lord your God shall choose in your tribe; there you shall offer burnt offerings, and there you shall do all that I command you today."

The Catholic replied: You have put forward an excellent testimony, and one well suited to your salvation: "Take heed to yourself that you do not offer burnt offerings in every place you see, but in the place which the Lord your God shall choose in your tribe; there you shall offer burnt offerings, and there you shall do all that he commands you." Hear, then, which is the chosen place, and which tribe of the Lord is proclaimed. In the hundred and thirty-first psalm you have: "For the Lord has chosen Zion; he has chosen it for his dwelling. This is my resting place for ever and ever; here I will dwell, for I have chosen it." Again in the hundred and twenty-first psalm: "Our feet were standing in your courts, O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which is built as a city. For there the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord, as a testimony to Israel." This is the chosen place, this the sanctified mountain, this the city set on a mountain so that it cannot be hidden, this the Catholic root, this the fruitful vine spread far and wide, which cries out in Ecclesiasticus and says: "In Zion I was established, and in Jerusalem is my power." For thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and the forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. You would be right to rebuke me if you remained in this inheritance. But since you do not remain in this inheritance of God the Father, and do not serve as a soldier in this tribe of Christ the King, why do you, a deserter, reproach a soldier? Why do you, the guilty one, upbraid the innocent? And I say to you: Take heed to yourself that you do not offer in every place — that is, in every heresy — saying, "God is here, and God is there too," but in the place which the Lord your God shall choose in your tribe — that is, in his tribe — there you shall offer your burnt offerings, and there you shall do all that has been commanded you. Do this, and you will live.

The Donatist said: So that cannot be called baptism which a confusion of waters has scattered, which malice has separated from the fountain of the Church, which a barren wave has dried up, which has seen neither an angel nor found a prophet able to heal it — just as, in the fourth book of Kingdoms, the most holy Elisha drove death out of the deadly waters, healed them, and by his fertilizing word let them flow toward abundant offspring: "And the men of the city said to Elisha: Behold, the situation of the city is good, as you, my lord, see, but the waters here are bad and barren. And Elisha said: Bring me a new earthen vessel and put salt in it. And they brought it, and he went to the source of the waters and threw in the salt and said: Thus says the Lord: I have healed these waters, and there shall be no more death or barrenness in them. And the waters were healed to this day."

The Catholic replied: Thanks be to God the Father, who has faithfully fulfilled in us what he showed would come. Thanks, I say, to God the Father, who sent to our Jericho — that is, to this world — not only angels, not only prophets as before, but his own Son, namely the Lord of the angels and the prince of the prophets, to drive out death and heal the barrenness of the waters, that is, the unfruitfulness of the nations. He took an earthen vessel, that is, a body of human frailty; he put salt in it, that is, he filled it with divine wisdom; he threw it into the water, that is, he went down into the Jordan; by his going down he healed the waters, that is, by his coming he redeemed the nations; and by his fertilizing word he gathered the Church from the nations and spread it far and wide in abundant offspring. Whoever does not see that this has been fulfilled in us is blind; whoever does not believe it is mad. Look at the abundant offspring: tell me where this Church is not; tell me where yours is to be found, except in a corner of Africa, badly gathered up like a useless cutting. Where it was cut off from this Church, there it has remained; it could not spread any further, because, cut off from the root, it withered at once.

The Donatist said: One city received the substance of the Saviour's water; one widow, together with her children, received the gift of oil. Nor did the prophet hand out the divine favour indiscriminately, but only to her whom he knew to have a single vessel of oil, as the truth of the book of Kingdoms proves: "And a woman, one of the wives of the prophets, cried out after Elisha, saying: Your servant my husband is dead, and you know that your servant feared God. And behold, those to whom I owe money have come to take my two sons as slaves. And Elisha said: What shall I do? Tell me what you have in your house. And she said: Your handmaid has nothing in the house except one vessel of oil. And Elisha said: Go, borrow vessels from outside, from all your neighbours, many vessels; then go in and shut the door upon yourself and your sons, and fill the vessels with oil, and pay your debt." For Elisha acted according to the outlines of true baptism. And because I do not approve of your baptism, I therefore perform the exorcism of breathing upon your faithful.

The Catholic replied: Why, everyone does what you do. They all breathe out over the faithful, while each claims for itself the one sacrament of baptism. When you find someone like that, will you not seize him, will you not hold him, will you not bind him with that same chain? Or, having recognized the pirate's mark, will you let him go off safe and sound, so that he may carry on the same trade alongside you?
Fulgentius said: Far be it from me to let him go, since God has said: "Compel them all to come in, so that my house may be filled." He who said "all" made no exception.
Augustine replied: What, then, will you do?
Fulgentius said: I will teach him that my church is the most certain.
Augustine replied: On what grounds? Will you show that Christ, who received all nations from the Father, has been left with only a small part of Africa?
Fulgentius said: I will say that it consists of a few.
Augustine replied: What if his church also has few? For compared with the Catholic Church, they all have few.
Fulgentius said: I will show that the true church is the one that suffers persecution, not the one that inflicts it.
Augustine replied: What if his church also has never inflicted persecution at all?
Fulgentius said: I will point out, following the apostle, that my church alone has no wrinkles or spots.

Augustine replied: It will at once be proved to have them. For it is written: "No one is clean from filth, not even if his life on earth has lasted but a single day." But why say more? Suppose you catch him and hold him by whatever cleverness you like: how do you receive a man who has perhaps rebaptized your faithful, who has extinguished the Holy Spirit in the heart of a believer?
Fulgentius said: I hold him fast, I breathe the exorcism upon him, and I baptize him with true water for the forgiveness of sins.

Augustine replied: How do you forgive his sins, when it is written that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit cannot be forgiven, for ever? But let us leave that aside and consider another point. Say to the Maximianist, your rival, what you said to me: "How can another have baptism, if it has been granted to me alone? Or if you claim it was handed over into your own right, why do you approve someone else's?" And this Maximianist too will answer: "How can another not have it, when you yourself have proved that it was granted to me just as to you? For you received my Christians and clergy, baptized or ordained outside your church, in full standing, without any change to their baptism or their rank!" This was raised against you in the proceedings before Marcellinus, and you were quite unable to refute it.
Augustine replied again: If you are just, why is your judgement inconsistent? Why do you receive the Maximianist, yet breathe the exorcism upon my faithful?
Fulgentius said: Because he was mine.
Augustine replied: And you were mine. Why do you persist in being merciful toward your own schismatic, yet unmerciful and implacable toward a Catholic?
Fulgentius said: You have sinned more, and so punishment is dealt out to you differently.

Augustine replied: What then? Do you use baptism as a punishment, and is what is promised for salvation handed out by you as a penalty? If in baptism you do not forgive offences but chastise sins, if in the water you do not set free but scourge, you openly show yourself to be a pirate. But tell me, how have I sinned more? What have I done?
Fulgentius said: You handed over the sacred books and sacrificed to idols.
Augustine replied: Prove it. I did not do it; you are pinning your own deeds on me.
Fulgentius said: Your father did it.
Augustine replied: I know no father except God. For it is written: "Call no one on earth your father, for you have one Father, who is in heaven."
Fulgentius said: By your father I mean Caecilian. He handed over the books, he offered incense, he committed every evil.

Augustine replied: Read it out: who accused him, who convicted him, who condemned him to his face? But suppose he did what he did not do: shall I, the son, be condemned for the father, when it is written: "The soul of the father is mine, and the soul of the son is mine. The soul that sins, it alone shall die"?
Fulgentius said: You, his son, did not indeed hand over the books, but you persecuted us.

Augustine replied: I certainly did not do it, though I believe my people may have done it. I ask the reason why. What if you deserved it? For it is no sin to persecute the wicked. Indeed, we read that the wicked were persecuted both by the saints and by the Holy of Holies, the Lord himself. For the demons, unable to bear the Lord's persecution, cried out: "What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come to destroy us?" Paul punished Elymas the magician with blindness and handed a blasphemer over to Satan; Peter struck dead the liars Ananias and his wife Sapphira, and pursued Simon the magician until he destroyed him by death. And David too, speaking in the person of Christ, cries out and says: "I will pursue my enemies and overtake them, and I will not turn back until they fail. I will afflict them, and they will not be able to stand." So not everyone who has suffered persecution is at once to be considered righteous; but whoever has suffered for righteousness' sake is truly blessed, as Peter says: "For what glory is there if, when you sin, you endure being beaten? But if, when you do good, you suffer and endure it patiently, this is grace before God."
Fulgentius said: The saints you mention did not obtain edicts from secular judges, as your people did.

Augustine replied: Either it is lawful or it is not. If it is lawful, it is not fitting to grumble about what is lawful; if it is not lawful, correct your own crime while you may. For, as the official records show, you persecuted your own schismatics, the Maximianists, with the authority of secular judges, the support of various town councils, and the enforcement of various detachments of soldiers, through defenders of the church appointed for the purpose, so as to drive them out of their basilicas. You who rebuke me, why do you not first correct yourself?
Fulgentius said: We took the basilicas from our schismatics so that we might restore them to the true Church.

Augustine replied: Our people did the same to you: they took them from their schismatics and handed them over to their Catholic mother. What your people did for the peace of Donatus, ours did for the peace of the body of Christ.
Fulgentius said: You are the schismatics, who both offered incense and handed over the sacred books.

Augustine replied: Let us become weak to the weak, so that we may win the weak. Let me grant what I know cannot be: the party of Donatus has conquered the whole of Christ; the African in his corner has shut out the whole world; one nation has condemned all the nations; the cutting has cut itself off from the vine and lopped the branches off the trees. Even so, you should at least have kept what your predecessors laid down concerning us: not to rebaptize, but to set free through penance the souls of those who, as you suppose, have gone astray. Reread the decrees of your fathers, and see what they decided must be done about traditors, those who offered incense, and schismatics, when they had come to Carthage in conspiracy against Caecilian. Your Marcianus, among others, gave a judgement which the seventy who were present certainly approved, since they did not reject it. "In his Gospel," he said, "the Lord says: I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he cuts off and throws away, and every one that abides in me and bears fruit he prunes. Just as fruitless branches are cut off and thrown away, so those who have offered incense and the traditors, who are abhorrent to God, cannot remain in the Church of God unless, having acknowledged their wailing, they are reconciled through penance. Therefore one must not communicate with Caecilian, who was ordained in schism by traditors."

This is the settled judgement of your fathers. Suppose — God forbid — that we did hand over the books, that we did offer incense, that we did commit schism: why do you transgress the commandment of your elders in order to establish your own traditions? "Just as fruitless branches," he says, "are cut off and thrown away, so those who have offered incense, the traditors, and those ordained in schism by traditors cannot remain in the Church of God unless, having acknowledged their wailing, they are reconciled through penance" — through penance, not through rebaptism. If you will deign to, at least let your own leaders win you over. Either confirm their decrees and lay aside your own inventions, or, if you want your own rulings to stand, declare that they were in error. If truth reigns among you, why is your tradition at odds with itself? The Saviour speaks thus in his Gospel: "Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste." And therefore, since your kingdom is divided in religion, destruction must follow upon the division. Amen.
